name: BASE
statement: BASE trades ACID's strict consistency for a basically-available, soft-state system that becomes consistent only eventually.
meaning: BASE — Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent — describes a consistency model, coined as a chemical pun opposing ACID’s "acid," for large distributed systems that favour availability and partition tolerance over immediate consistency. A basically available system responds to nearly all requests even if data is stale; its state is "soft" because it may change over time as updates propagate; and it becomes consistent only after updates finish propagating to all replicas.
mechanism: Systems achieve BASE semantics by relaxing synchronous replication: writes are accepted locally or on a subset of replicas and acknowledged immediately, then propagated asynchronously, with conflict resolution such as last-write-wins, vector clocks, or read-repair reconciling divergent copies over time.

examples.text: Dan Pritchett, an eBay architecture Technical Fellow, introduced BASE in his 2008 ACM Queue article "BASE: An Acid Alternative" to describe eBay’s approach to scaling partitioned databases.
Amazon’s Dynamo key-value store is a canonical BASE-style system, favouring availability and using eventual consistency across replicas.
Apache Cassandra, a wide-column NoSQL store, offers tunable consistency but defaults to BASE-style eventual-consistency semantics.

whyItMatters: BASE gave engineers a named, legitimate alternative to ACID for building the high-availability, horizontally-scaled systems needed by large web applications, directly shaping the NoSQL movement of the 2000s–2010s.
limits: BASE is an informal, descriptive heuristic rather than a proven theorem, and its terms — "basically available," "soft state" — are not formally defined the way CAP’s or ACID’s terms are, leading to inconsistent usage across the industry.
misreadings: BASE is sometimes wrongly treated as older than or foundational to the CAP theorem; Pritchett’s naming (2008) came after Brewer’s CAP conjecture (2000), and BASE is best understood as a practitioner-friendly gloss on CAP-driven eventual-consistency designs rather than an independent theorem.
origin: Coined by Dan Pritchett of eBay in his 2008 article "BASE: An Acid Alternative," ACM Queue.

sources.text: Pritchett, "BASE: An Acid Alternative," ACM Queue 6(3) (2008). — the origin, author, year, and core trade-off claim.
